extracted.intended_audience: patent lawyers, judges, and law students (practitioners and students of patent law)
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts and summarizes substantive legal standards governing patentability, infringement, defenses, remedies, jurisdiction, evidence, and related procedural and equitable doctrines from a comprehensive legal treatise on patent law.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentability requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: To be patentable a technical solution must be (1) new, (2) involve an inventive step, and (3) be industrially applicable; novelty, inventive skill, and utility are essential; invention must fall within the patentable classes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess novelty (absence of prior patent/publication/use), inventive skill (non-obviousness/evidence of inventive activity), and utility (practical usefulness; immorality or danger defeats utility). See related sections on patentable classes, novelty, and utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Novelty (prior patent/publication/use)
rubrics_metrics.description: Denial of the novelty of the patented art or instrument is a principal defence (Fifth Defence). Novelty defeated by prior patent, prior publication, or prior practical use.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evidence for novelty-defense includes prior patent, prior publication, prior use; prior publication must describe a complete practical invention. Secret prior use has specific treatment; requisites and notice requirements apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Utility of the invention
rubrics_metrics.description: Utility (usefulness) is essential to patentability; absent if the invention is immoral or dangerous; degree of utility is immaterial so long as the invention can be made useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Utility may be shown by use and sale; actual (not merely comparative) utility required. Utility is often a question for the jury and is evidence of inventive skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable classes / subject-matter eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Defence may be that the patented art or instrument is not within the patentable classes; theory, abstractions, and pure scientific theory are not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether claimed subject-matter fits statutory/recognized patentable classes (machine, manufacture, composition, process); exclude theories, laws of nature, principles unless reduced to practice in patentable form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sufficiency of specification / written disclosure
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguity or defective disclosure in the specification can be a defence (Twelfth Defence; fraudulent concealment or misrepresentation in specification also a defence).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specification must adequately describe invention and enable practice; fraudulent or misleading disclosures require notice; ambiguity may invalidate or limit claims; reissue can cure some errors in description.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ambiguity and excessiveness in claims
rubrics_metrics.description: Ambiguity in the claims (Fourteenth Defence) and excessive claims (Thirteenth Defence) are defensible defects; claims must be clear and limited to proper scope.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims are strictly construed; ambiguity may be raised as a defence and affect infringement analysis. Excessive claims (over-claiming) can render patent vulnerable to attack or reissue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement: definition and identity requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement defined; no infringement exists unless the invention unlawfully used is identical with that protected by the patent. Identity must be identity in the idea of means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine identity by comparing ideas and means, not merely form; identity may result from use as well as original construction. Later-issued patents do not necessarily avoid identity analysis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acts constituting infringement (making, using, selling)
rubrics_metrics.description: Infringement can occur by unlawful making, using, or selling of the patented invention; infringement may embrace acts of making, use, and sale as a single tort.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess whether defendant's acts fall within statutory categories; possession/exposure for sale/advertising alone may not constitute infringement absent making/using/selling as defined.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temporal and territorial limits of infringement
rubrics_metrics.description: No infringement can be committed before the issue of the patent; infringement can be committed only within the area of the United States (with special rules for Government use).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Consider date of issue and geographic scope when evaluating infringement claims; governmental use has distinct rules and potential compensation obligations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement by actors (licensees, co-owners, agents, contractors, workmen)
rubrics_metrics.description: Various parties (licensees under express or implied licenses, co-owners, assignees, agents, contractors, common carriers, employees) may be liable for infringement under different doctrines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Liability depends on status: express licensees, implied licensees, co-owners, agents acting within scope; distinguish voluntary agents/workmen (may infringe) from those having no option (may not).

rubrics_metrics.name: Infringement of combination patents (elements, sub-combinations, parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: For patents on combinations, unauthorized use of elements, sub-combinations, or part of the combination may constitute infringement depending on identity and functional equivalence.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyze whether accused device/practice appropriates the idea/means of the combination; unauthorized use of essential elements or sub-combinations can infringe; use of part only may or may not infringe depending on role.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defences: denial of inventive act or origin (First and Second Defences)
rubrics_metrics.description: First Defence: deny that the patented art/instrument is the result of an inventive act; Second Defence: deny that it resulted from the inventive act of the alleged inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof may require evidence of origin, reduction to practice, and performance by alleged inventor; burden and types of admissible evidence specified in evidence sections.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defence: priority / first inventor (Third Defence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Denial that the alleged inventor was the first and true inventor; priority disputes are a defence to infringement.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Priority requires proof of earlier inventive acts/priority dates; special notice and pleading requirements may apply; interferences and related procedures govern competing claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defence: abandonment to the public
rubrics_metrics.description: Abandonment of the invention to the public is a defence (Seventh Defence) — patentees who voluntarily and unrestrictedly disclose may forfeit rights.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate whether disclosure was unrestricted; statutory exceptions exist (e.g., two-year protection prior to application); evidence and notice rules apply for asserting abandonment as a defence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defence: prior patent or publication
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior patent or prior publication anticipating the claimed invention is a defence (evidentiary treatment of prior publications and patents detailed).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior publication must sufficiently describe a complete practical invention; notice may be required; treat prior patents/publications as primary evidence against novelty.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defence: prior use
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior practical use of the invention by others may defeat novelty and thus be a defence; requisites and proof of prior use are outlined.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior use must be practical (not merely theoretical or secret) and typically requires notice; courts examine extent, timing, and publicness of prior use.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defence: lack of legal title or ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: Denial of legal title in the plaintiff (Seventeenth Defence) or challenges to the grant/legality of the patent are available; plaintiff must be legal owner at date of infringement to sue at law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess chain of title, assignments, recording; equitable interests vs legal title; transfer and assignment formalities govern standing; recording and proper assignment are important.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defence: estoppel, release, res judicata, statute of limitations
rubrics_metrics.description: Defences include estoppel (Twenty-Third), release (Twenty-Fourth), res adjudicata (Twenty-Fifth), and statute of limitations (Twenty-Second).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These are procedural/ equitable bars — examine prior conduct, prior judgments, releases, and statutory limitation periods; notice requirements and pleading form vary by defence.

rubrics_metrics.name: Pleadings and notice requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Pleadings in actions at law require specific allegations (inventive act, grant, title, infringement, damages); certain defences (fraudulent specification, prior patent/publication, prior use, abandonment) require notice with formal requisites.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow statutory and case-law rules for form and service of notice; failure to give required notice may preclude certain defences; rules differ under various patent acts and procedural eras.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence: burden, admissibility, expert testimony, patent as evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules of evidence in patent actions govern admissibility, competency, credibility, expert witnesses, documentary evidence; the patent may serve as evidence but is interpreted by the court.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Burden of proof allocated (plaintiff typically proves infringement/validity), expert testimony admissibility and classes defined, judicial notice of certain facts possible; evidence as to state of the art at date of invention is critical.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedy at law vs equity; adequacy of legal remedy
rubrics_metrics.description: Whether to grant equitable relief depends on adequacy of remedy at law; equitable jurisdiction complete when equitable relief is necessary; no equity jurisdiction where adequate remedy at law exists.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess prospective injury, irreparable harm, availability of damages, ownership status, and whether discovery or equitable grounds are essential. The nature of plaintiff's benefit-taking (licenses vs exclusive practice) affects remedy choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunctions (preliminary and perpetual) — standards and grounds
rubrics_metrics.description: Preliminary injunctions guided by established rules: generally grantable only to prevent prospective injury where no adequate remedy at law exists and typically only when patent is valid, title in plaintiff, and danger of infringement exists; perpetual injunctions granted when appropriate at final hearing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of validity may rely on prior judgments, public acquiescence, admissions; courts consider irreparable injury, laches, estoppel, defendant's good faith or patent, balance of harms, and potential disastrous consequences if injunction granted; bond and accounting may be ordered in lieu.

rubrics_metrics.name: Computation of damages and profits
rubrics_metrics.description: Rules distinguish nominal and actual damages; measures vary with mode plaintiff takes benefit (licenses vs exclusive practice). Profits in equity and damages at law differ in theory and computation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Damages may be measured by license fees (where monopoly enjoyed by licensing), direct evidence of injury, indirect evidence (lost sales, market impact), receipts and savings as minuend for profits, entire market value rule for certain product sales; interest and increased damages may apply; counsel fees not generally recoverable as damages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accounting for infringer's gains (profits) and burden of proof
rubrics_metrics.description: Equity can compel an infringer to account for unlawful gains; plaintiff bears burden to show receipts or savings; courts distinguish modes of infringement when computing profits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Take into account receipts, savings, commissions, repairs, duration of infringement, apportionment among multiple infringers, and corporate liability. Masters' reports and exceptions subject to review; detailed accounting procedures apply.

rubrics_metrics.name: Jurisdiction (federal exclusivity and diversity)
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal courts have exclusive jurisdiction over cases arising under the patent laws; federal jurisdiction also where parties are citizens of different states though not exclusive in all such cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Identify whether case 'arises under' patent laws (affects monopoly); determine proper venue (circuit/district), original jurisdiction of circuit courts, and procedures for actions against corporations and others.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unpatented inventions and protection of trade secrets
rubrics_metrics.description: Inventor's right to preserve secret rests on natural law; forcible or fraudulent discovery/disclosure of a secret invention violates inventor's rights and is actionable; right to secret protected though invention not patentable.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Remedies include tort actions and injunctions; confidential communications, breach of trust, and misuse by recipients are actionable; unrestricted public disclosure forfeits right unless statute protects (e.g., two-year pre-application protection).

rubrics_metrics.name: Transfer, assignment and title to patents
rubrics_metrics.description: Title to a patent is created by issue of the patent and transferable typically only by written assignment; transfers may convey invention and monopoly or only certain rights; recording affects conclusiveness.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assignments must be in writing; transfers covering whole U.S. or specified territory have rules; the assignee of record at issue may hold legal title; equity can enforce or cure defects; estoppel and recordation implications discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reissue and surrender to correct errors
rubrics_metrics.description: Errors in stating the patent or claims may be cured by surrender and reissue; reissue and re-examination have defined effects and limitations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reissue procedures, grounds (e.g., claim excessiveness, error in description), time limits, and effects on rights and prior art are set out; undue delay and reissue doctrines discussed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preliminary injunction evidence weight: prior judgments and public acquiescence
rubrics_metrics.description: Prior judgments and public acquiescence can be evidence of patent validity for injunctive relief; weight depends on identity of parties, identity of issues, availability of testimony, and circumstances of prior judgment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate prior judgments (court level, collusion, consent, Patent Office decisions) and manifestations of public acquiescence; weigh against other evidence like admissions and scope of prior findings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Local and procedural rules in equity and law (joinder, pleadings, amendments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Detailed rules govern parties plaintiff/defendant, joinder and misjoinder, amendments, cross-bills, supplemental bills, demurrers, pleas, answers, and special defences in equity and at law.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow proper procedural form (e.g., sue in own name, service, appearance), note special defenses peculiar to equity (laches, estoppel), and conform to requirements for feigned issues, jury trials, and interlocutory decrees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expert witnesses and technical evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: Classes of expert witnesses, their distinctions, and when expert testimony is admissible are specified; experts often needed to explain state of the art and inventive step.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Admissibility depends on relevancy, competency, and whether testimony assists the trier of fact; expert opinion used to show state of the art at date of invention, novelty, and inventive skill.

rubrics_metrics.name: Statutory and common-law defenses concerning patent validity (fraud, illegality, want of title)
rubrics_metrics.description: Defences include fraudulent specification, illegality of letters-patent, denial that letters-patent were issued in conformity with law, and want of title in plaintiff.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These defenses often require notice; they implicate both statutory requirements and equitable doctrines; courts analyze procedural history, compliance with patent statutes, and possible remedies including repeal or reissue.
